claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially has a high-temperature BCC phase.
Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed primarily by thermodynamic free-energy minimization.
CALPHAD simulations can predict the relevant free-energy minimization for this alloy.
The high-temperature BCC state is metastably maintained by kinetic barriers.
Controlled cooling causes transformation when the CALPHAD-predicted free-energy difference overcomes kinetic barriers.
Local chemical ordering and solute redistribution alter the alloy's free-energy landscape.
Local chemical ordering and solute redistribution enable phase transformation when thermodynamic driving forces become dominant.
As temperature decreases, the free-energy difference between the high-temperature BCC phase and the equilibrium phase or phases increases.
A phase transformation occurs when the energetic benefit of atomic rearrangement exceeds the kinetic barriers.
Controlled cooling will produce a distinct transformation from BCC to equilibrium secondary phases near the CALPHAD-predicted transition temperature.
The secondary phases formed during cooling may include FCC or intermetallic phases.
Samples maintained at high temperature will retain the metastable BCC state.
The prediction applies when cooling rates and isothermal holds allow sufficient time for the thermodynamically predicted transformation.
Extremely rapid cooling may suppress or alter the predicted transformation behavior.
Non-uniform temperature control may cause behavior that departs from the prediction.
Microstructural defects and residual stresses may alter the transformation temperature and identity of the secondary phases relative to CALPHAD predictions.
Failure to observe a transformation near the CALPHAD-predicted range would falsify the hypothesis.
A transformation temperature significantly different from the CALPHAD prediction would falsify the claim that thermodynamics primarily governs phase stability.
